To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) state effects on children’s later mathematical development are substantially smaller than trait effects, (b) trait effects on children's mathematical development are substantially larger than residualized state effects, and (c) residualized trait effects on childrens mathematical development are substantially greater than state effects.

(1) individual differences in children's mathematical achievement are substantially related across time, (2) these relations are not due to children's early mathematical competency directly affecting their later mathematical competency, and (3) the relations between children's mathematical achievement at different times are due to children's stable characteristics related to mathematical learning throughout development (i.e., traits) more so than to children's mathematical competency at the previous time point (i.e., states).
individual differences in mathematical knowledge are more related to stable traits than to states.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of individual differences in the development of mathematics.
the role of individual differences on children’s mathematical learning and development.

the question of how much of the variance in children's mathematical development can be explained by their stable characteristics (traits) and how much can be explained by the effects of prior knowledge (states).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects are not as strong as one might have expected, but that they are not negligible either.
the longitudinal relations between children's mathematics achievement and their mathematics achievement in much later years are due to stable characteristics related to learning across time.
the effect size of state variables (e.g., early mathematical knowledge) is smaller than that of trait variables (e.g. general cognitive ability, motivation) on children’s mathematical learning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the longitudinal relations between children's early mathematics achievement and later mathematics achievement are not due to the direct effects of early mathematics achievement on later mathematics achievement.

children’s early mathematics learning is a better indicator of stable individual characteristics that influence learning throughout development than it is of direct effects of children’s early mathematics competency on children’s later mathematical competency.
children’s mathematical development is more an indicator of underlying, stable characteristics than of direct effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the effects of early mathematics achievement on later achievement should be interpreted with caution, because they may be due to underlying characteristics of children, rather than direct effects of early mathematics on later achievement.
the longitudinal relation between early and later mathematical achievement is not a direct relation.
the effects of early educational interventions on children’s mathematical learning may be more limited than previously thought.
